summary: Defines the COMPRESS extension, which allows an IMAP connection to be compressed efficiently. This can save bandwidth, helpful on slow links. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Packing your suitcase tightly so you send less stuff over the road.

questions: how to compress an imap connection
how does imap compression work with tls
subtitle: How an IMAP client and server agree to squeeze everything they send each other with DEFLATE.

tldr.problem: IMAP traffic is bulky and repetitive, and bandwidth can be scarce, but IMAP had no standard way to compress a connection.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises COMPRESS=DEFLATE. The client sends one COMPRESS DEFLATE command, and after the tagged OK both sides compress everything they send with DEFLATE.
tldr.outcome: The extension adds one command and no new responses. It is a Proposed Standard, and a client that supports both is told to prefer TLS compression when it is available.

today: RFC 4978 is a Proposed Standard from August 2007, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goal
sections.content:
RFC 4978 defines the COMPRESS extension for IMAP. Its goal is to reduce the bandwidth an IMAP connection uses. A server that supports it announces one or more capability names of the form COMPRESS= followed by an algorithm name.

The RFC says COMPRESS offers much better compression efficiency than PPP compression or modem-based compression. It can be used together with TLS, SASL encryption and VPNs.
sections.eli5: The goal is simple: send less data. The server says which packing method it knows, and the client can ask to use it.

sections.title: Why Compress in IMAP and Why DEFLATE
sections.content:
TLS can also compress (see RFC 3749), and when it does, any protocol on top of it benefits. The RFC lists what IMAP COMPRESS offers instead: it is easy to implement for both servers and clients, and it can use intimate knowledge of the IMAP state machine to tune the compression algorithm's parameters dynamically and aggressively. The trade-off is that COMPRESS is specific to IMAP.

To help interoperation, the RFC wants as few algorithms as possible, so it defines only one: DEFLATE from RFC 1951, described as standard, widely available and fairly efficient.

Servers that advertise COMPRESS SHOULD also advertise TLS DEFLATE compression. Clients MAY use either, but if both are supported it is RECOMMENDED that the client choose TLS compression.
sections.eli5: There are two places to pack things: inside the secure tunnel or inside IMAP itself. Both work, but if both are offered, the tunnel is the one to pick.

sections.title: The COMPRESS Command
sections.content:
The command takes one argument, the name of the compression mechanism, and the only one defined is DEFLATE. It produces no untagged responses. The result is one of three:

  • OK: the server will compress its responses and expects the client to compress its commands.
  • NO: compression is already active via another layer.
  • BAD: the command is unknown or invalid, the argument is unknown, or COMPRESS is already active.

The client MUST NOT send further commands until it has seen the result. On OK, the client MUST compress starting with the first command after COMPRESS. On BAD or NO it MUST NOT turn compression on. The server MUST begin compressing immediately after the CRLF that ends the tagged OK, so responses before that stay uncompressed.

If the server answers NO because the same mechanism is already active, for example through TLS, it MUST send the response code COMPRESSIONACTIVE, and the human-readable text SHOULD say which layer compresses.

Each side may pick its own compression level, since the compressor trades speed against quality while decompression has little trade-off.
sections.eli5: The client asks, wait for the server to say yes, and from the next message on both sides send packed messages. If the server says it is already packing, the client should not ask twice.

sections.title: Combining with TLS and SASL
sections.content:
When COMPRESS is combined with TLS or a SASL security layer, the sending order MUST be first COMPRESS, then SASL, and finally TLS. Data is compressed first, then signed or encrypted by the SASL layer if one was negotiated, then signed or encrypted by TLS if one was negotiated. On receiving, the order MUST be reversed.

This guarantees that data is compressed before it is encrypted, no matter in which order the client issues COMPRESS, AUTHENTICATE and STARTTLS.
sections.eli5: You squash the clothes into the suitcase first and lock it afterwards. Locking first would leave nothing to squash.

sections.title: Compression Efficiency
sections.content:
This section of the RFC is informative, not normative. Upstream traffic is easy: clients send the same few commands repeatedly, which any repetition-exploiting algorithm handles well. The exception is APPEND, where large literals may be surrounded by flushes.

Downstream traffic is harder because it mixes several kinds of data that confuse dictionary-based compressors: IMAP responses, email headers, body text and attachments. Responses, headers and text compress well. Attachments are a problem because the dictionary built from IMAP does not help, a few formats such as .gz, .zip and .jpg do not compress with DEFLATE at all, and base-64 hides the 8-bit file format from the compressor.

The RFC suggests several improvements:

  • A client can use BINARY (RFC 3516) and FETCH BINARY instead of FETCH BODY. The author reports 5% to 40% better results, depending on the attachment.
  • A server can send a Z_FULL_FLUSH at the start and end of large non-text literals, leaving small literals alone. A possible boundary is 5k.
  • A server can lower the compression level to 0 at the start of a literal if its first two bytes are 0x1F 0x8B or 0xFF 0xD8 (JPEG), keeping it at 1-5 otherwise.

With zlib, the RFC says deflateInit2(), deflate(), inflateInit2() and inflate() suffice, and that windowBits must be in the range -8 to -15.
sections.eli5: Plain text squeezes down nicely, but things that are already squeezed, like photos and zip files, will not shrink. The server can skip wasting effort on those.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar adds a compress command to command-auth, a COMPRESS= capability (multiple COMPRESS capabilities are allowed), a single algorithm DEFLATE, and the response code COMPRESSIONACTIVE. Strings are case-insensitive and implementations MUST accept them that way.

Because of the syntax of capability names, future algorithm names must be atoms.
sections.eli5: The rules spell out exactly how to write the new command and the new words, so everyone writes them the same way.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single line: the same as for TLS compression (RFC 3749). The RFC adds nothing of its own.

For IANA, COMPRESS=DEFLATE was added to the list of IMAP capabilities.
sections.eli5: The safety notes just point to the notes for the other way of packing. IANA wrote the new name in the official list.
